Goals 0 of 9

Janus

One tile, two true colors

The Mermin-Peres square on two qubits

Every square here has two true colors. Read it along its row and it shows one color. Read it down its column and it can show another. At least one square always changes, and the physics guarantees it.

For example: Your website's Buy button uses one of these squares. One visitor sees it teal, the next sees it coral, and both pages still follow all six color rules, so the design never breaks.

Goal: Find a world where only one square changes.

The science, for the curious

Each tile is a quantum observable. Read it with its row or with its column and it can take a different color, and no fixed coloring could ever satisfy all six rules at once.

or press Space

Mermin's Dare

Try to color it classically

After N. David Mermin, 1990

A puzzle with no solution. Put a plus or a minus on each square so every row and column multiplies out to the sign it asks for. You will always break at least one rule.

For example: It's like a sudoku that can't be finished. The best anyone can do is 5 of the 6 rules. A quantum computer gets all 6, every time, because its squares don't carry fixed answers.

Goal: Get 5 of 6 rules by flipping squares yourself.

The science, for the curious

Give every tile a fixed value, +1 or −1. Every row must multiply to +1, columns one and two to +1, and column three to −1. Tap tiles to flip them.

-

Why it fails

Multiply all nine values row by row and you get +1. Multiply them column by column and you get −1. Same nine numbers, two answers, so one rule always breaks.

Quantum measurement escapes this because a tile has no value until it is read, and the value it gets depends on its partners. That is contextuality, and Qontext turns it into color.

Checked by computer

All 512 fixed assignments were searched. The best any of them can do is 5 of 6 rules.

Unity Wheel

Harmony is quantum phase

Roots of unity on the color wheel

Pick how many colors you want and they spread out evenly around the color wheel, like the hours on a clock. Every other room in the Atelier uses these colors.

For example: Choose 3 colors and a teal starting point and you get a balanced trio of teal, coral and gold, ready for a brand. Drop in a photo and the wheel starts from its main color.

Goal: Save a harmony you like to your library.

The science, for the curious

A d-level quantum system has phases spaced evenly around a circle. Put them on the hue wheel and you get complementary, triadic, tetradic and beyond, all perfectly balanced.

Fringe

Mix colors like waves

A Mach-Zehnder interferometer for color

Mix two colors the way waves of light mix. Turn the dial and color slides from one output to the other. Nothing is lost: what leaves one side shows up on the other.

For example: Put a color and its opposite in, like blue and orange. At the right turn of the dial one output fades to plain gray while the other glows twice as strong.

Goal: Turn the dial until one output fades to gray.

The science, for the curious

Each color becomes a wave: hue is its phase, chroma its amplitude. Two colors meet at a beam splitter and leave through two ports. Shift the phase and the ports trade color while the total stays constant.

Port 1 across a full turn of the dial. Drag along the band, or use the dial below.

Color in, color out

Color going in-
Color coming out-
Share in port 1-

Energy is conserved, so color removed from one port appears in the other. Opposite phases cancel to neutral gray in one port and double up in the other.

Pentacle

The pentagram palette

The KCBS test on one qutrit

Five colors on a star. Colors joined by a line can never both be picked, and the size of each dot is its chance. Ordinary rules cap the total chance at 2. Quantum rules go higher.

For example: Use it for five chart categories. Colors joined on the star sit far apart on the color wheel, so no two connected slices ever look alike.

Goal: Turn the knobs back to the top score, 2.236.

The science, for the curious

Five quantum events where neighbours on the star can never both happen. Any classical model keeps their total chance at 2 or below. The right qutrit state reaches the square root of 5.

Total chance

Point size shows each event's chance. Tilt to zero for the maximum. Linked hues sit 144 degrees apart, so neighbouring colors never look alike.

Spooky Pair

Entangled assets

A Bell pair and the CHSH game

Two designs, one light and one dark, share a linked pair of quantum coins. Each design picks a style and flips its coin, and the two coins land in step more often than any two separate coins could.

For example: A light landing page and its dark twin. When both are calm their accent colors tend to match. When both are bold they tend to clash. Two separate dice can't keep that promise this well.

Goal: Set both to Bold and catch them clashing.

The science, for the curious

A light asset and a dark asset share an entangled pair. Each picks a style, and the accent it gets is its measurement outcome. Their accents agree and clash more reliably than any two independent rules allow.

Unpaintables

Shapes no coloring can finish

Kochen-Specker shape packs

3D shapes made of arrows. The rule sounds easy: in every group of arrows at right angles, light up exactly one. For two of these shapes nobody, and no computer, can follow that rule everywhere. Something always breaks.

For example: Export one as an SVG or a 3D file and you have a logo or a small sculpture that is mathematically impossible to color in, with the broken spot showing every time.

Goal: Find the one shape that can be colored.

The science, for the curious

Each shape is a set of directions in space. A classical coloring must light exactly one direction in every perpendicular set and never light two perpendicular directions. For Peres 33 and Cabello 18 that is impossible, and the broken set always shows.

Notary

Prove it was real

Colors from a real quantum computer

Normally your colors come from a simulation running in this browser. Notary lets you take them from a real quantum computer instead, and gives you a stamp anyone can use to check them.

For example: Print “measured on IBM Quantum” on a poster. The stamp's fingerprint lets anyone confirm the colors came from those exact results, and nobody can quietly swap them.

Goal: Get your first stamp.

  1. 1

    See it with an example

    Open a real run: 20,480 measurements made on IBM's ibm_kingston quantum computer on 12 October 2026. Or try practice results from a computer that imitates a noisy chip, stamped as a practice run.

  2. 2

    Run it on a real quantum computer

    Probe, our free command line tool, runs the same color circuits on IBM Quantum and saves the results as a file. IBM's free plan is enough.

    For developers: the commands 
    pip install './python[ibm]'
qontext-probe --noisy              # try it on your computer first
qontext-probe --ibm least_busy     # run on IBM Quantum
  3. 3

    Bring your results here

Take your colors with you

Your colors, ready for your own work

Take your colors into your own work. Choose where they're going, then copy or download. Each square comes with both of its colors, so your project can use either reading.

For example: Building a website? Choose A website, press Copy, paste it into your stylesheet, and your buttons and headings use these colors right away.
